config.title: Controlled Input

intro.title: Controlled Input
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple form with a text input field that displays its current value in real-time. You will learn the concept of a controlled input, where React state becomes the single source of truth for the input's value. The main technologies involved are React's useState hook and TypeScript for type safety. By the end, you'll understand how to synchronize form data with component state, a fundamental pattern in React applications.
intro.usecase: Controlled inputs are essential for any interactive form where you need real-time validation and immediate user feedback. You'll use them in login/registration forms to validate email formats and password strength as users type. They're also critical in dashboard filters where changing one input should instantly update charts and tables, or in e-commerce product configurators where selecting options updates pricing dynamically. This pattern gives developers complete control over form state and behavior.

objectives: Define a component state variable to store input value using the useState hook
Implement an event handler function to update state when input changes
Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the shape of props for reusable controlled input components
Utilize the onChange event attribute to connect input elements to state update handlers
Construct controlled input components by binding the value attribute to state variables
Control form submission behavior by preventing default browser actions with event.preventDefault()
Access input values from state variables to display or process user data
Modify input behavior by applying conditional styling based on state values
Use the value attribute to implement input clearing functionality by resetting state to empty string
Implement validation logic by comparing current input values against defined criteria
Apply controlled input patterns to different HTML form elements (text, email, textarea)
Return structured JSX that includes both input elements and their associated state management logic

steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:

import React, { useState } from 'react';

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building a controlled input component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but check your import statement. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main component function
steps.instruction: Create a function component named ControlledInput that returns JSX.Element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component function that will eventually return JSX. For TypeScript, you can specify the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a ControlledInput component function defined, ready to contain the controlled input logic in later steps.
successCriteria: The code must include a function or const named ControlledInput that returns JSX.Element (or implicitly returns JSX).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ControlledInput component function. This is the foundation for building our controlled input.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a component named ControlledInput that returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component function wasn't created correctly. Please create a function named ControlledInput that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize state for the input value
steps.instruction: Inside your ControlledInput component, declare a state variable named 'inputValue' and its setter using useState, initialized as an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to provide the generic type <string> and initialize with ''.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a string state variable
const [inputValue, setInputValue] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a state variable 'inputValue' initialized to an empty string, ready to store the user's typed input.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the inputValue state with useState. This creates a reactive variable that will store the user's input and trigger re-renders when it changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the state variable 'inputValue'? Did you initialize it with an empty string? Did you include the TypeScript generic <string>?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to call useState with an empty string as the initial value, name the variable 'inputValue', and include the TypeScript generic <string>.

steps.title: Define the change handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your ControlledInput component, define a function named handleChange that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter and updates the inputValue state with the event's current value.
steps.hint: The function should use the setInputValue function from useState to update the state. Access the input value from event.target.value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleChange function that properly updates the inputValue state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The code must include a function named handleChange that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter and calls setInputValue with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleChange function that will update the state when the input changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your handleChange function properly accepts the event parameter and updates the state with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleChange function is missing or doesn't match the expected structure. Make sure it takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter and calls setInputValue with the event's value.

steps.title: Add the input element
steps.instruction: Inside the div wrapper, add an input element with type='text' and placeholder='Type something...'.
steps.hint: Use the JSX <input> tag with the required attributes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Add an input element with basic attributes
<input type="text" placeholder="Enter your name" />
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now render a text input field with a placeholder.
successCriteria: The input element must be inside the div, have type='text', and placeholder='Type something...'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the input element with the correct attributes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input element, but check if it has both type='text' and placeholder='Type something...'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input element is missing or has incorrect attributes. Make sure it's inside the div with type='text' and placeholder='Type something...'.

steps.title: Connect input value to state
steps.instruction: Inside the input element, add a value attribute and set it to the inputValue state variable.
steps.hint: Use the value prop on the input element and reference the state variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of binding input value to state
<input value={inputValue} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The input element will have its value bound to the inputValue state, making it a controlled input.
successCriteria: The input element includes a value attribute set to the inputValue state variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully bound the input's value to state, making it a controlled input.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the value attribute is set to the inputValue state variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input element should have a value attribute connected to the inputValue state variable.

steps.title: Wire the change handler to the input
steps.instruction: Connect the input's onChange event to the handleChange function you defined earlier.
steps.hint: Add an onChange attribute to the input element and set it equal to your handleChange function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The input element will have an onChange attribute that calls handleChange when the user types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the onChange event to your handler function. Now when the user types in the input, the handleChange function will be called to update the state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the onChange handler isn't quite correct. Make sure you're using the exact function name 'handleChange' and the proper syntax onChange={handleChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The onChange handler isn't properly connected. Remember to add onChange={handleChange} to the input element to connect it to your change handler function.
